name: Charles Darwin
role: English naturalist and originator of the theory of evolution by natural selection (1809–1882)
summary: Darwin was a naturalist who wrote little directly on politics. His recorded positions are a firm hatred of slavery, support for the Union and for prosecuting Governor Eyre, a regulated defence of animal experiments, a rejection of biblical revelation, and, in the Descent of Man, views on civilisation, race and the sexes that were conventional for his time. He declined to advocate cutting poor relief despite its eugenic cost, and his views on most economic and constitutional questions are unrecorded.

notes: Searched his own books, autobiography and letters (local Project Gutenberg corpus) plus the Darwin Correspondence Project for slavery, civil war, empire, poor relief, inheritance and primogeniture, suffrage, religion, vivisection, socialism and political parties. He avoided politics and said his political opinions were formed rather by the way than with serious thought, so most statements are null. Statements on socialism and welfare are not settled by his words: he only remarked that the supposed link between socialism and natural selection was a foolish idea. The early Beagle remark that tyranny suited South American states better than republicanism was about those states only and is not used. His statements on civilisation changed little over his life.
